architecture_fit.reason: Evidence for K includes amphiphilic block copolymers (PEG-PLL-PLLeu, L15K6) and polypeptide nanoparticles (chiral poly(phe)-block-poly(lys)), closely matching the target amphiphilic binary poly(amino acid) architecture. R evidence is limited to PTD fusions and nanofibers, lacking direct block copolymer analogues.

vaccine_mechanism_fit.reason: K evidence demonstrates robust dendritic cell maturation, antigen cross-presentation, CTL responses, and in vivo tumor inhibition, often outperforming alum (E002, E022). R evidence shows strong T-cell activation and MHC presentation but lacks explicit cross-presentation and direct adjuvant superiority.

delivery_safety_balance.reason: K evidence shows excellent biocompatibility with low hemolysis and high cell viability (E014, E015, E016), while R evidence indicates context-dependent safety (some hemolysis at high doses) but superior endosomal escape (E032). Both have acceptable trade-offs; no clear advantage for this project.

uncertainties: Direct head-to-head comparison of K vs R in the exact project architecture is lacking.
Endosomal escape advantage of R (E032) may be critical for biomacromolecule delivery but safety concerns are mitigated in specific formulations.
Cross-presentation evidence for K is robust but limited to OVA model; generalizability to other antigens is assumed.

architecture_fit.reason: K has direct evidence of block copolymer and nanoparticle architectures (e.g., PEG-PLL-PLLeu, P_L-K block copolymer, hyperbranched PLL in lipopolyplex) that closely match the target amphiphilic binary poly(amino acid) carrier. R evidence primarily uses simple polyarginine chains or fusion proteins, lacking clear block copolymer examples.

vaccine_mechanism_fit.reason: K evidence includes robust dendritic cell maturation, antigen cross-presentation, and antitumor efficacy in block copolymer nanoparticle vaccine systems (e.g., P_D-K-OVA, PEG-PLL-PLLeu micelles), directly relevant to the tumor-vaccine carrier. While R also shows strong immune responses, K's systems are more architecturally aligned with the project.

delivery_safety_balance.reason: R has superior intracellular delivery and endosomal escape evidence (E032, E033) but has some safety concerns (hemolysis, complement activation). K has cleaner safety data (low hemolysis, high cell viability) but less detailed intracellular handling. The balance is even for this criterion.

uncertainties: Most evidence for both candidates uses protein/peptide antigens; less direct evidence for mRNA or other biomacromolecules beyond one K study (E001).
Intracellular handling (endosomal escape) evidence for K is less explicit than for R, which may affect cross-presentation efficiency in vaccine context.
Safety data for K at the specific chain lengths and architectures used in block copolymers is not fully characterized.

project_context.target_system: amphiphilic binary poly(amino acid) tumor-vaccine carrier
project_context.role_interchangeability_context: K and R are regarded by the project team as potentially replaceable cationic blocks; the existing experimental route uses K.
project_context.use_of_context: This is a project-continuity prior, not literature evidence. It is used only if the literature-based K-vs-R project-fit comparison is tied or insufficient.

basis: Direct head-to-head comparison in polypeptide nanoparticle nanoadjuvants (E093, E096) shows that poly(D-lysine)-containing nanoparticles (P_D-K-OVA) more robustly induce dendritic cell maturation, antigen cross-presentation, and adaptive immune response compared to poly(L-lysine)-containing nanoparticles (P_L-K-OVA), achieving 94.9% tumor inhibition in a B16-OVA melanoma model.
These direct comparisons are in the specified systems (polypeptide, nanoparticle, nanoadjuvant, dendritic-cell, vaccine) and are given highest evidentiary priority per the instructions.

The conflicting direct comparisons in aluminum oxyhydroxide nanoadjuvants (E094, E097) involve lysine only as a structure-directing agent, not as the primary immune component, and are therefore less directly relevant to lysine chirality in polypeptide/nanoparticle systems.
uncertainties: Direct comparison evidence is limited to a single model antigen (OVA) and one tumor model (B16-OVA melanoma).

A conflicting direct comparison in aluminum oxyhydroxide nanoadjuvants (E094, E097) shows L-lysine-induced material yields better outcomes, but that system uses lysine only as a chiral inducer, not as the active polymer component.
No direct L-vs-D lysine comparison in human cells or clinical systems is available.

basis: Direct head-to-head comparison in chiral polypeptide nanoparticle nanoadjuvants (E093, E096) shows that D-lysine-containing P_D-K-OVA more robustly induces dendritic cell maturation, antigen cross-presentation, and adaptive immune response than L-lysine-containing P_L-K-OVA, achieving 94.9% tumor inhibition in a melanoma model versus weaker effects for the L-lysine variant.
This direct comparison is in the most relevant context: polypeptide nanoparticles as nanoadjuvants for vaccines, directly addressing dendritic cells and antigen presentation.

Although an indirect comparison in aluminum oxyhydroxide nanoadjuvants (E094, E097) shows L-lysine-derived material outperforms D-lysine-derived material, that system uses lysine only as a structure-directing agent, not as a polymeric component, and is less directly applicable to the query's specified polypeptide and nanoparticle systems.
uncertainties: The two direct comparisons (polypeptide nanoparticles vs. aluminum oxyhydroxide nanoadjuvants) give opposite preferences; the aluminum oxyhydroxide study suggests L-lysine-associated material may be better in that specific mineral-adjuvant context, but its relevance to polypeptide/nanoparticle vaccine systems is limited.
All direct comparisons involve lysine in polymeric or templating contexts, not free lysine.
Evidence is limited to a single model antigen (OVA) and a single tumor model (B16-OVA) in the most relevant direct comparison.
No human in vivo data are available for either chirality.
